lessons.title: Preparing for Lambing Season
lessons.body:
Preparing for lambing starts at least six weeks before the first ewe is due. In most of Africa, lambing coincides with the end of the dry season or the start of the rains, so plan around your local climate. First, condition-score your ewes: they should be at 3 to 3.5 on a 5-point scale. Thin ewes (score 2 or less) need extra feedâgive 250â500 g of maize or sorghum bran per day, plus good hay. Fat ewes (score 4+) risk difficult births, so reduce concentrates. Vaccinate all ewes against pulpy kidney and tetanus 4â6 weeks before lambing. Also drench for internal parasites using a product like albendazole, following the dosage on the label.

Next, prepare a clean, dry lambing area. A 3 m x 3 m pen can hold 8â10 ewes. Spread dry straw or wood shavings. Provide a creep areaâa small, sheltered corner with a heat lamp or a simple wooden box lined with dry grassâfor newborn lambs to escape cold and drafts. In hot climates, ensure shade and ventilation. Have on hand: iodine for navels, a clean bucket, soap, towels, a stomach tube and syringe for feeding colostrum, and a lambing jack or ropes for difficult births. Keep a notebook to record dates and any problems.

Feed ewes well in late pregnancy. The last 6 weeks, the lamb grows 70% of its birth weight. Give 500 gâ1 kg of a mix of maize, cottonseed cake, and minerals per ewe per day, plus free-choice hay. Provide clean water at all times. Separate ewes that are close to lambing into a maternity pen at night. Check them every 3â4 hours during the day. Look for signs: restlessness, pawing the ground, a water bag appearing. Most ewes lamb without help, but be ready to assist if no progress after 30 minutes of straining. Keep records of which ewe lambs, when, and how many lambs. This helps you manage future breeding and culling.

lessons.title: Normal and Difficult Births
lessons.body:
A normal birth (lambing) happens in three stages. Stage 1 lasts 2â6 hours: the ewe separates from the flock, paws the ground, and may bleat. Stage 2 is active labour: strong contractions, and the water bag appears. The lamb should be delivered within 30â60 minutes. Normal presentation is two front feet first, with the head resting between them. Once the head is out, the rest follows quickly. Stage 3 is passing the placenta, usually within 2â4 hours. Do not pull on the placenta; let it come naturally. If the ewe strains for more than 30 minutes with no progress, or if you see a tail or only one foot, it is a difficult birth.

For a difficult birth, wash your hands and arms with soap and water. Use a mild disinfectant. Lubricate with vegetable oil or clean grease. Gently insert your hand to feel the lambâs position. If the head is turned back, push the lamb slightly back and cup the head to bring it forward. If legs are bent, find the legs and pull them into the birth canal. Work slowly. If you cannot correct it in 10 minutes, call for help or a vet. Use a lambing rope or clean towel to grip the legs and pull gently downwards and towards the eweâs hocks when she strains. Never pull with force; you can tear the ewe. After a difficult birth, give the ewe antibiotics (e.g., oxytetracycline) as directed by a vet to prevent infection.

After birth, clear the lambâs nose and mouth of mucus. If the lamb is not breathing, rub it briskly with a towel or straw. Hold it upside down for a few seconds to drain fluid. Dip the navel in iodine. Ensure the lamb breathes within 30 seconds. For twins or triplets, help the ewe dry them and ensure each gets colostrum. Keep the ewe and lambs in a clean pen for 24â48 hours. Watch for retained placenta (more than 12 hours) or a ewe that is off feedâthese need veterinary attention. Record any difficult births to avoid breeding from that ewe again if the problem is hereditary.

lessons.title: Colostrum Management
lessons.body:
Colostrum is the first milk a ewe produces after lambing. It is rich in antibodies, fat, and energy. Lambs are born with no immunity; they must absorb antibodies from colostrum within the first 6 hours of life. After 24 hours, the gut closes and antibodies cannot pass. So timing is critical: the lamb must suckle within 30 minutes to 1 hour of birth. A newborn lamb needs 50 ml of colostrum per kg of body weight in the first 6 hours. For a 4 kg lamb, that is 200 ml. Then feed 200 ml every 4â6 hours for the first 24 hours. If the lamb is weak, use a stomach tube. Measure the tube from mouth to last rib, mark it, and pass gently. Give colostrum at body temperature (38â39Â°C).

If the ewe dies or rejects the lamb, use colostrum from another ewe, or frozen colostrum from a previous lambing. You can also use cow colostrum, but it is less concentrated; add 1 egg yolk per 500 ml to boost energy. Commercial colostrum replacers are available in farm supply shops. Never feed boiled or heated colostrum above 40Â°Câit destroys antibodies. If you must store colostrum, refrigerate for up to 24 hours or freeze in small bags for up to 6 months. Thaw in warm water, not a microwave.

For orphan lambs, feed colostrum via a bottle with a teat. If the lamb wonât suck, tube-feed. After the first 24 hours, transition to milk replacer or goat milk. Feed 200â250 ml per feeding, 4 times a day for the first week. Always sterilise bottles and tubes. Keep a chart for each lamb: birth weight, time of first colostrum, amount given. Lambs that get enough colostrum are 5 times less likely to die in the first month. In Africa, where diseases like pneumonia and scours are common, colostrum is your cheapest insurance. If a ewe has mastitis or no milk, treat the ewe and hand-feed the lamb. Never leave a lamb to starveâit will die within 12 hours.

lessons.title: Orphan Lamb Care
lessons.body:
Orphan lambs come from ewes that die, reject their lamb, or have no milk. In Africa, many orphan lambs are caused by poor nutrition, disease, or difficult births. Your goal is to keep the lamb warm, fed, and clean. First, move the lamb to a dry, draft-free pen. A simple wooden box with a heat lamp (or a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel) works. The lamb needs an environment of 25â30Â°C for the first week. If it is shivering, warm it slowlyârubbing with a towel and warm water bottles. Never feed a cold lamb; warm it first.

Feeding: Use a bottle with a lamb teat. Feed colostrum for the first 24 hours as described in Lesson 3. After that, use a milk replacer specifically for lambs, or goat milk. Mix according to the labelâusually 1 part powder to 4 parts warm water (40Â°C). Feed 200â250 ml per feeding, 4 times a day for the first week, then 3 times a day. By week 4, reduce to 2 feedings and offer creep feed (a mix of maize, soybean meal, and minerals) and clean hay. Always feed at the same times. Keep a chart: date, time, amount. Weigh the lamb weekly. A healthy orphan gains 150â200 g per day. If it loses weight, increase feed or check for disease.

Hygiene is critical. Wash bottles and teats after every feeding with hot soapy water. Rinse well. Store milk replacer in a cool, dry place. Orphan lambs are prone to scours (diarrhoea) and pneumonia. If scours occur, reduce milk amount for one feeding and give oral rehydration solution (1 teaspoon salt, 1 teaspoon sugar in 1 litre water). If pneumonia (coughing, rapid breathing) appears, call a vet for antibiotics. Also, orphan lambs need company. If possible, pen them with a gentle older lamb or a quiet ewe. Social isolation causes stress. After 2 weeks, introduce them to a small group of other lambs. By 8 weeks, they should be eating solid food and can be weaned. Record all treatments and weights. Good care turns a weak orphan into a productive sheep.

lessons.title: Weaning Strategies
lessons.body:
Weaning is when you separate lambs from their mothers. In Africa, most lambs are weaned at 8â12 weeks of age, but it depends on breed and feed. For meat breeds like Dorper, wean at 8â10 weeks. For wool breeds, 10â12 weeks. The lamb should weigh at least 12â15 kg and be eating solid feed well. Weaning too early (before 6 weeks) causes stress and poor growth. Weaning too late (after 16 weeks) drains the ewe and delays her next pregnancy. Plan to wean when the lambs are strong and the pasture is good.

Before weaning, prepare the lambs. From 2 weeks of age, offer creep feedâa high-protein mix (16â18% protein) of maize, soybean meal, and minerals. Also provide clean, fresh hay. Lambs learn to eat by watching their mothers. By 6 weeks, they should be eating 200â300 g of creep per day. At weaning, move the lambs to a clean, well-fenced paddock with good grass and shade. Leave the ewes behind. The lambs will bleat for 1â2 days, but they settle. Provide plenty of water and the same creep feed they are used to. Do not change feed suddenly. For the first week after weaning, feed 300â400 g of creep per lamb per day, plus hay. After 2 weeks, you can reduce creep and let them graze.

Weaning management: Keep lambs in a group of similar size to reduce bullying. Check daily for signs of stress: droopy ears, off feed, or diarrhoea. If any lamb is sick, isolate and treat. Weigh a sample of lambs at weaning and again 4 weeks later. A good growth rate is 150â200 g per day. If growth is poor, check for parasitesâdrench with albendazole. Also, vaccinate lambs against pulpy kidney at weaning and give a booster 4 weeks later. Ewes should be dried off: reduce their feed and water for 3â5 days to stop milk production. Check udders for mastitis. After weaning, ewes can be prepared for the next breeding season. Record weaning weights and dates. This data helps you select the best lambs for breeding and cull poor performers.

lessons.title: Growth and Development Monitoring
lessons.body:
Monitoring growth is how you know if your lambs are healthy and your management is working. Start by weighing lambs at birth. A normal birth weight for most African breeds is 2.5â4 kg. Weigh weekly for the first 8 weeks, then every 2 weeks until 6 months. Use a hanging scale or a bathroom scaleâweigh yourself, then hold the lamb and subtract. Record weights in a notebook or on a simple chart. A healthy lamb gains 150â250 g per day in the first month. By 8 weeks, it should weigh 12â18 kg. If a lamb gains less than 100 g per day, investigate: is the ewe producing enough milk? Are parasites present? Is feed adequate?

Body condition scoring (BCS) is a hands-on tool. For lambs, feel the spine and ribs. A score of 3 (on a 5-point scale) is ideal. If you can feel sharp bones, the lamb is thinâincrease feed. If you cannot feel bones, it is fatâreduce concentrates. Also monitor height and body length: a lamb should double its birth weight by 8 weeks and triple by 16 weeks. Measure heart girth (around the chest just behind the front legs) with a tape measure. A gain of 1 cm in heart girth per week is good. Keep records for each lamb. This helps you spot slow growers early.

Health checks go with growth. Watch for signs of disease: coughing, diarrhoea, lameness, or dull coat. Common problems in lambs include coccidiosis (bloody diarrhoea), pneumonia, and internal parasites. Drench lambs for worms every 4â6 weeks if pasture is wet. Vaccinate for pulpy kidney and tetanus. If a lamb stops growing, isolate it and check its temperature (normal is 38.5â39.5Â°C). Treat according to vet advice. At 3 months, select lambs for breeding or sale. Keep the fastest growers; cull the slow ones. In Africa, where feed can be scarce, monitoring growth ensures you invest in the best animals. Good records also help you plan sales and breeding. Weigh, score, and recordâevery week.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a ewe six weeks before lambing?
quiz.explanation: Ewes should be in moderate condition (3 to 3.5) to support lamb growth without birthing difficulties.

quiz.q: Which vaccine should be given to ewes 4â6 weeks before lambing?
quiz.explanation: This vaccine protects both the ewe and the newborn lamb via colostrum.

quiz.q: How often should you check ewes close to lambing during the day?
quiz.explanation: Frequent checks allow you to assist if there are complications.

quiz.q: What is the normal presentation for a lamb at birth?
options: B) One front leg and head
C) Two front feet and head between them
quiz.explanation: This is the correct position for an unassisted birth.

quiz.q: How long should a ewe be in active labour before you intervene?
quiz.explanation: If no progress after 30 minutes of straining, assist or call for help.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after a lamb is born?
options: D) Separate it from the ewe
quiz.explanation: Iodine prevents navel infections.

quiz.q: How soon after birth must a lamb receive colostrum?
quiz.explanation: Antibodies are absorbed best within the first 6 hours.

quiz.q: How much colostrum does a 4 kg lamb need in the first 6 hours?
quiz.explanation: The requirement is 50 ml per kg of body weight, so 4 kg x 50 ml = 200 ml.

quiz.q: What temperature should colostrum be fed at?
quiz.explanation: Body temperature is ideal; too hot destroys antibodies, too cold causes chilling.

quiz.q: How long can colostrum be stored in a refrigerator?
quiz.explanation: Refrigeration at 4Â°C keeps colostrum good for up to 24 hours.

quiz.q: What is a good substitute for ewe colostrum if none is available?
options: A) Cow colostrum with egg yolk
quiz.explanation: Cow colostrum is less concentrated, so add egg yolk for energy.

quiz.q: How should you thaw frozen colostrum?
quiz.explanation: Microwave or high heat destroys antibodies; warm water is safe.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for a newborn orphan lamb's pen?
quiz.explanation: Orphan lambs need warmth; 25â30Â°C prevents chilling.

quiz.q: How often should you feed a 2-week-old orphan lamb?
quiz.explanation: Feed 4 times daily for the first weeks to meet nutritional needs.

quiz.q: What is a sign of scours in an orphan lamb?
quiz.explanation: Scours is diarrhoea, often caused by unclean feeding equipment.

quiz.q: What should you do if an orphan lamb has scours?
quiz.explanation: Rehydration prevents dehydration; reduce milk for one feeding.

quiz.q: At what age are most lambs weaned in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 8â12 weeks balances lamb development and ewe recovery.

quiz.q: What is creep feed?
quiz.explanation: Creep feed is a nutritious mix offered to lambs from 2 weeks of age.

quiz.q: How much creep feed should a lamb eat per day by 6 weeks of age?
quiz.explanation: By 6 weeks, lambs should be eating 200â300 g of creep daily.

quiz.q: What should you do with ewes after weaning to dry them off?
options: B) Reduce feed and water for 3â5 days
quiz.explanation: Reducing feed and water helps stop milk production and prevents mastitis.

quiz.q: What is a good growth rate for a lamb in the first month?
quiz.explanation: Healthy lambs gain 150â250 g daily under good management.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh lambs in the first 8 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Weekly weighing helps track growth and spot problems early.

quiz.q: What does a body condition score of 3 mean for a lamb?
quiz.explanation: Score 3 is moderate; bones are felt but not sharp.

quiz.q: What is a common internal parasite problem in lambs?
quiz.explanation: Coccidiosis causes diarrhoea and poor growth, common in wet conditions.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature of a lamb?
quiz.explanation: This range indicates a healthy lamb; fever suggests infection.

quiz.q: When should lambs be vaccinated against pulpy kidney?
options: B) At weaning and 4 weeks later
quiz.explanation: Vaccination at weaning and a booster provides immunity.

quiz.q: What is the best way to select lambs for breeding?
quiz.explanation: Fast growth indicates good genetics and health.

quiz.q: How can you measure a lamb's heart girth?
options: B) Around the chest behind front legs
quiz.explanation: Heart girth correlates with weight and growth.

quiz.q: What should you do if a lamb is not breathing after birth?
options: A) Rub it briskly with a towel
B) Hang it upside down for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Stimulating the lamb helps clear airways and start breathing.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in lambing?
options: B) To track growth, health, and breeding
quiz.explanation: Records help make informed decisions on feeding, culling, and breeding.
